comparison.a: Candidate A is strong on requirements/architecture articulation and provides a solid acceptance-test list (AT1–AT23), plus clear HITL interrupt triggers and synthesis warnings/open questions; however, it is less operationally decomposed into stage-by-stage milestones with deliverables/exit criteria and has less explicit milestone-level acceptance-test coverage mapping.
comparison.b: Candidate B is more implementation-ready and closure-oriented because it decomposes the O1 linear pipeline into concrete milestones with deliverables and exit criteria, explicitly maps/evaluates acceptance-test coverage across milestones, and operationalizes governance via decisioning and milestone gates; it also more explicitly calls out the big-bang downside (no partial-freeze) as a key consequence.

evidence.note: Differentiator: operational decomposition—Candidate A has a single high-level milestone block.
Differentiator: operational decomposition—Candidate B defines M1–M7 with deliverables and exit criteria aligned to the linear pipeline.
Differentiator: testability—Candidate A provides AT1–AT23 but without an explicit milestone-by-milestone coverage evaluation.
Differentiator: testability—Candidate B explicitly summarizes acceptance-test coverage by milestones.
Differentiator: governance—Candidate A defines HITL interrupt triggers.
Differentiator: governance operationalization—Candidate B explicitly decides/configures high HITL strictness (DEC3).
Differentiator: clarity on key blockers—Candidate A warns about multiple blocking open questions impacting enforceability.
Differentiator: clarity on big-bang consequence—Candidate B explicitly flags lack of partial-freeze as a budget-risk consequence.

payload.notes: Winner B due to better closure readiness from milestone-level operationalization and explicit acceptance-test coverage mapping, while maintaining a similarly conservative O1/big-bang governance posture.
